Deny means to push something away — either by saying it isn't true, or by refusing to let someone have it. Think of it as a word that involves rejection or refusal, but the kind of rejection depends on the situation.

1. To say that something is not true

This is the most common use. When you deny a claim, an accusation, or a statement, you are saying: "No, that is false. That did not happen."

  • She denied cheating on the exam.
  • The politician denied taking any bribes.
  • He denied that he had ever met her.

Here, someone is being accused of something — or a claim is being made about them — and they are pushing back against it by saying it isn't true. The word carries a feeling of defense. There is a claim against you, and you are fighting it.

Notice: denying doesn't tell us whether the person is actually telling the truth. A person can deny something truthfully (when they genuinely didn't do it) or falsely (when they did do it but don't want to admit it). The word itself is neutral on this — it only tells us that someone is saying "that's not true."

2. To refuse to give something to someone

Here, deny means to withhold something — to not let someone have what they want or need.

  • The court denied his request for bail.
  • She was denied entry into the building.
  • They were denied the chance to say goodbye.

In this sense, deny often has a slightly unfortunate or unfair feeling to it. It suggests that someone wanted or deserved something, but it was taken away from them or not given to them. You'll notice this meaning frequently in legal, official, or formal situations.

This trips up a lot of learners, so pay close attention:

After "deny," you must use the -ing form of a verb, not the "to + verb" form.

✅ He denied stealing the car. (correct)
❌ He denied to steal the car. (wrong)

✅ She denied knowing about the plan. (correct)
❌ She denied to know about the plan. (wrong)

This is because "deny" belongs to a group of verbs — like admit, avoid, suggest, consider — that are always followed by the -ing form (called a gerund). Never use "to + verb" after "deny."

You can also follow "deny" with a that clause:

  • He denied that he had stolen the car.

And you can use it with two objects (deny someone something):

  • They denied him his rights.
  • The judge denied her the opportunity to speak.

You can also deny yourself something, which means to voluntarily go without it — often as an act of self-discipline or sacrifice.

  • She denied herself sweets for an entire month.
  • He denied himself the pleasure of sleep to finish the project.

Here, there is no other person involved. You are the one choosing to hold yourself back from something you want. This use carries a sense of willpower or restraint.

In older, more literary or religious language, you can also "deny" a person — meaning to disown them, to refuse to acknowledge that you know them or are connected to them.

  • He denied his own father to avoid embarrassment.
  • She denied her past and started a new life.

This is a more dramatic and personal form of denial. It isn't just about refusing a request — it's about turning your back on someone, pretending they don't exist in your life.

"Deny" is not a neutral word. It almost always carries a sense of conflict, pressure, or something being at stake.

When it means saying something is false, there is usually a battle of truth involved — one side claiming something, and the other pushing back.

When it means refusing to give, there is usually a power dynamic — someone in a position of authority is keeping something from someone who needs or wants it.

This is why "deny" often appears in serious, high-stakes contexts: courts, politics, investigations, arguments, and moral decisions.

The phrase in denial (or in a state of denial) is very common and important. It comes from psychology and means:

refusing to accept an unpleasant truth, even when the evidence is clear.

  • She's in denial about how serious her illness is.
  • He's in denial — he refuses to believe his marriage is failing.

When someone is "in denial," they are not consciously lying. They are unconsciously protecting themselves from a painful reality by refusing to acknowledge it. It's a defense mechanism.

This phrase is now used so widely in everyday speech that it has gone far beyond its psychological origins. You'll hear it constantly.
Common Collocations (Words "Deny" Is Often Paired With)

These are the natural combinations you'll encounter and need to know:

  • flatly deny — to deny something completely and directly, with no hesitation: He flatly denied any involvement.
  • strongly deny — to deny something with emphasis and force: The company strongly denied the allegations.
  • vehemently deny — to deny with great passion or anger: She vehemently denied the charge.
  • categorically deny — to deny something in every possible way, leaving no room for doubt: He categorically denied ever meeting her.
  • deny access / entry / permission — to refuse to allow someone in or to let them do something.
  • deny responsibility — to refuse to accept blame.
  • deny a request / claim / allegation / accusation — these are the standard objects you'll see paired with the word.

Deny vs. Refuse:
Refuse means you won't do something. Deny means you won't give something (or you say something is false). "She refused to help" vs. "She denied him help." Both words involve saying no, but refuse focuses on an action you won't perform, while deny focuses on withholding something from someone.

Deny vs. Reject:
Reject is more absolute and final. You reject something entirely — a job application, a proposal, a person. Deny is often softer and more specific: you deny a particular request, or you deny a particular claim. Rejection suggests the whole thing is unwanted; denial is more targeted.

Deny vs. Contradict:
Contradict means to say the opposite of what someone said. Deny means specifically to say that a claim against you is false. If someone says "the sky is green" and you say "no, it's blue," you are contradicting them. If someone says "you stole the money" and you say "no, I didn't," you are denying it.

To deny something is to:

  1. Say it is not true (in the face of an accusation or claim), or
  2. Refuse to let someone have or do something, or
  3. Withhold something from yourself voluntarily.

The word always carries a sense of saying no to something — whether that "no" is directed at a truth, at a person's request, or at your own desires. It lives in the territory of conflict, defense, and refusal.
